Recurrent Networks & LSTMs

Networks that remember what came before

Text, speech, prices and heartbeats arrive one step at a time, and what a step means depends on the steps before it. A recurrent network reads a sequence the way you do: one item at a time, carrying a running state forward. The network in the figure has read a million characters of Shakespeare, one letter at a time, and nothing else. Type the start of a line and press Write: it continues letter by letter. Hover any letter to see what else it considered.

The idea
One small network, applied at every step, passing a state forward
The problem
Gradients fade, or explode, as they travel back through time
The fix
Gates that decide what to write, keep and read: LSTMs and GRUs

The idea

Why order needs memory

“Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” use the same three words. A model that sees only which words are present (a bag of words) cannot tell them apart; a network with a fixed input window cannot see past the window’s edge. A recurrent network instead keeps a state h, a short summary of everything read so far, and updates it at every step. The simplest possible memory is a single number that keeps a fraction a of its old value and adds the new input. Click the timeline to place input pulses (click a pulse to remove it), then turn the memory dial.

\[ \begin{aligned} h_t &= a\,h_{t-1} + x_t \\ \Rightarrow\ h_t &= \sum_{k=1}^{t} a^{\,t-k}\, x_k \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: each step, the state keeps a share a of what it held and adds today’s input. Unfold the recursion and the state is a weighted sum of every input so far, where an input from t − k steps ago counts with weight at−k. For a < 1 old inputs fade geometrically; for a > 1 they grow without limit.
Say it“h-t is a times h-t-minus-one plus x-t; so h-t is the sum of a to the power t-minus-k times x-k.”
half-life of a memory
state at the last step

The recurrent cell

One rule, reused at every step

A real recurrent network does the same thing with vectors and a non-linearity. The state is a vector h; at each step a weight matrix W mixes the old state, a matrix U injects the new input, and tanh squashes the result into (−1, 1). The same W and U are used at every step, so one small set of weights can read a sequence of any length (Elman, 1990). Below, the state has two numbers, so you can watch it move in the plane. Each symbol pushes it in its own direction; W rotates and scales what was there. Press A, B and C to feed the network a sequence, then change W.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_t &= \tanh\!\big(W\,\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + U\,\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}\big) \\ \hat{\mathbf{y}}_t &= \operatorname{softmax}\!\big(V\,\mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{c}\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: new state = squash(mix of the old state + the current input + a bias). xt is the input at step t (here a one-hot code for A, B or C, so U xt simply picks that symbol’s column of U). An optional read-out V turns any state into a prediction – for a language model, a probability for every possible next character. W, U, V and the biases are the only weights, shared by every step.
Say it“h-t is tanh of W h-t-minus-one plus U x-t plus b; the prediction is the softmax of V h-t plus c.”
steps read
trace of the first symbol

Training

Unrolling through time

To train a recurrent network, draw it out: one copy of the cell per step, each passing its state to the next. This unrolled network is an ordinary deep network, as deep as the sequence is long, in which every layer shares the same weights. Backpropagation then works as usual and is called backpropagation through time (BPTT; Werbos, 1990). The catch is in the chain rule: a loss at the last step reaches an early state only by passing back through every step in between, and each step multiplies the signal by a Jacobian matrix. Below is the sequence you typed above, unrolled. Click any state hk to send the gradient back to it.

\[ \begin{aligned} L &= \sum_{t=1}^{T} L_t \\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} &= \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{h}_t}\, \frac{\partial^{+} \mathbf{h}_t}{\partial W} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the loss of a sequence is the sum of the losses at its steps. W is used at every step, so its gradient is a sum over steps; ∂+ means the direct effect of W at step t only, with the earlier states held fixed. ∂L/∂ht collects every route by which ht affects present and future losses.
Say it“The loss is the sum of the step losses; the gradient for W adds up, over every step, dL by dh-t times the direct effect of W on h-t.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_T}{\partial \mathbf{h}_k} &= \prod_{j=k+1}^{T} \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_j}{\partial \mathbf{h}_{j-1}} \\ &= \prod_{j=k+1}^{T} D_j\, W \\ D_j &= \operatorname{diag}\!\big(1-\mathbf{h}_j^2\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the route from step k to step T is a product of T − k Jacobians, one per step. Each is W, scaled down by tanh’s slope 1 − h² (between 0 and 1). Its size is what decides whether step T can learn anything from step k.
Say it“dh-T by dh-k is the product, from j equals k-plus-one to T, of D-j times W.”
steps back
size of ∂hT/∂hk
weights in the cell
layers in the unrolled net

The problem

Vanishing and exploding gradients

Shrink the cell to one unit and the product of Jacobians becomes a product of plain numbers, each equal to w times tanh’s slope. Multiply many numbers a little below 1 and you get almost nothing; a little above 1, and you get an explosion. Hochreiter (1991) and Bengio, Simard & Frasconi (1994) showed this is why plain RNNs struggle to learn anything that spans more than a few dozen steps: the learning signal from far back is drowned out by the signal from nearby. Turn the recurrent weight w, and switch tanh off to see the exploding case.

\[ \begin{aligned} h_t &= \phi(w\,h_{t-1} + x_t) \\ \left|\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_k}\right| &= \prod_{j=k+1}^{t} \big|w\,\phi'(w h_{j-1} + x_j)\big| \\ &\le |w|^{\,t-k} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: each step multiplies the gradient by |w| times the slope of the activation φ (for tanh the slope is 1 − hj², at most 1). If |w| < 1 the gradient must shrink geometrically. If |w| > 1 it can grow, but only while the unit is not saturated, because saturation flattens the slope.
Say it“The size of dh-t by dh-k is the product of w times phi-prime over the steps in between, and is at most w to the power t-minus-k.”
\[ \mathbf{g} \leftarrow \mathbf{g}\cdot\min\!\Big(1,\ \frac{\tau}{\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert}\Big) \]
Read it as: the standard cure for exploding gradients (Pascanu, Mikolov & Bengio, 2013): if the gradient vector is longer than a threshold τ, shrink it to length τ but keep its direction. It stops one huge step from wrecking the weights. It does nothing for vanishing gradients; those need a different design, which is what LSTMs are.
Say it“g becomes g times the smaller of one and tau over the length of g.”
gradient after 10 steps
after 50 steps

The fix

The LSTM’s gated memory

Hochreiter & Schmidhuber’s long short-term memory (1997) adds a second state, the cell c, that is changed only by addition and by a multiplication the network controls. Three gates, each a sigmoid between 0 and 1, decide: how much of the old cell to keep (forget gate f), how much of a new candidate g to write (input gate i) and how much of the cell to show as the output h (output gate o). When f is near 1 the cell is a conveyor belt: values ride along unchanged, and so does the gradient. Below is a one-unit LSTM whose weights are set by hand, so its gates obey flags you control. Click the grid to set write, erase and read flags, and move the mouse over the plot to inspect a step.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{f}_t &= \sigma(W_f\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + U_f\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_f) \\ \mathbf{i}_t &= \sigma(W_i\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + U_i\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_i) \\ \mathbf{o}_t &= \sigma(W_o\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + U_o\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_o) \\ \mathbf{g}_t &= \tanh(W_g\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + U_g\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_g) \\ \mathbf{c}_t &= \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \mathbf{g}_t \\ \mathbf{h}_t &= \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\mathbf{c}_t) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: four little layers read the same old output ht−1 and new input xt. Three of them are gates (sigmoids, between 0 and 1); one, g, proposes new content (tanh, between −1 and 1). ⊙ multiplies element by element. The cell update is the heart: keep a share f of the old cell, add a share i of the candidate. The forget gate was added by Gers, Schmidhuber & Cummins (2000).
Say it“The new cell is f times the old cell plus i times g; the output is o times tanh of the cell.”
\[ \frac{\partial c_T}{\partial c_k}\bigg|_{\text{cell path}} = \prod_{j=k+1}^{T} f_j \]
Read it as: along the conveyor belt (the cell’s own path from ck to cT) the gradient is multiplied by the forget gates and nothing else: no weight matrix, no squashing slope. If the network learns to hold f near 1, the gradient survives hundreds of steps. (Other paths, through the gates, add further terms; this one is the protected route.)
Say it“dc-T by dc-k is the product of the forget gates in between.”
cell at the inspected step
gradient kept since the last write

How the hand-set weights work

The input at each step is x = (value v, write flag W, erase flag E, read flag R), and the recurrent weights are zero, so each gate depends only on the flags: i = σ(8W − 4), f = σ(bf − 10W − 10E), o = σ(8R − 4), and the candidate is g = tanh(2v). A flag of 1 drives its gate to about 0.98; a flag of 0 to about 0.02. A trained LSTM learns weights like these from data, with the flags replaced by whatever in the input signals “store this” or “now is the time to use it”.

A lighter cousin

GRUs: two gates instead of three

Cho and colleagues (2014) found a simpler cell that keeps the main trick. The gated recurrent unit (GRU) has no separate cell: its state h is the memory. One update gate z does the jobs of both forget and input gates, since whatever share z of the state it rewrites, it keeps the other 1 − z, and a reset gate r decides how much of the old state the candidate may look at. There is no output gate: the memory is always on show. With a quarter fewer weights than an LSTM of the same width, it often learns just as well (Chung et al., 2014). Below is a hand-wired one-unit GRU on the same timeline. Set write flags, then slide the reset gate from “replace” to “accumulate”.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{z}_t &= \sigma(W_z\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + U_z\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_z) \\ \mathbf{r}_t &= \sigma(W_r\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + U_r\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_r) \\ \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t &= \tanh\!\big(W_h(\mathbf{r}_t \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1}) \\ &\qquad\quad + U_h\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_h\big) \\ \mathbf{h}_t &= (1-\mathbf{z}_t)\odot\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{z}_t\odot\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the new state is a blend: keep 1 − z of the old one, take z of a candidate. The candidate h̃ is a plain RNN step, except that the reset gate r first decides how much of the old state goes into it. Where z is near 0 the state passes through untouched, which gives the same protected gradient path as the LSTM’s cell.
Say it“h-t is one-minus-z times h-t-minus-one plus z times h-tilde, where h-tilde is tanh of W times r-times-h, plus U x, plus b.”

Playground

Who remembers longest?

Now train all three cells for real, in your browser, on a task built to need long memory. Each sequence starts with A or B, followed by a stretch of random filler symbols; at the very end the network must say which letter came first. Nothing in the filler helps, so the only useful learning signal has to travel back through the whole gap. Each cell has 8 units, the same data, the same optimiser (Adam) and the same starting seed. Choose a gap and press Race.

\[ \begin{aligned} L &= -\log p_\theta\big(s_1 \mid s_1, s_2, \dots, s_{G+1}\big) \\ s_1 &\in \{\text{A}, \text{B}\} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the loss is the network’s surprise at the right answer, read at the last step, after G filler symbols. Guessing gives p = ½, a loss of log 2 ≈ 0.693 and 50% accuracy. Getting below that needs a gradient that reaches step 1.
Say it“The loss is minus the log of the probability the network gives to the first symbol, after reading the whole sequence.”

Real-world project

Project: an LSTM that writes Shakespeare

Tiny Shakespeare (Karpathy, 2015) is 1,115,394 characters of Shakespeare’s plays in one plain-text file: speakers’ names, verse and prose, with 65 distinct characters. A character-level language model reads it one character at a time and, at every step, predicts the next one. We kept the first 90% for training and held out the last 10% (111,540 characters). Three networks of the same size, about 108,000 weights each, were trained offline in numpy with backpropagation through time over 100-character windows: a plain RNN with 270 units, a GRU with 150 and an LSTM with 128 (8,000 Adam steps of 32 windows each, about 25 passes over the training text). Their weights are embedded in this page, and every forward pass below runs in your browser.

1 · Score them on Shakespeare they never saw

The yardstick is bits per character: the average surprise, −log₂ p, at the true next character. A model that guesses uniformly among 65 characters scores log₂ 65 ≈ 6.02 bits; lower is better.

\[ \text{bpc} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} \log_2 p_\theta\big(x_{t+1} \mid x_{\le t}\big) \]
Read it as: run the model along the held-out text, carrying its state (x≤t means every character up to t), and average the surprise at each true next character. 2 bits per character means the model is, on average, as unsure as if it were choosing among 2² = 4 equally likely characters.
Say it“Bits per character is minus the average of log-two of the probability the model gave to each true next character.”

2 · Let it write

To write, the model turns its scores into probabilities with a temperature T, samples a character, feeds that character back in as the next input, and repeats. Low T sharpens the distribution (safe, repetitive text); high T flattens it (inventive, then garbled).

\[ p(x_{t+1} = k) = \frac{e^{s_k / T}}{\sum_{j} e^{s_j / T}} \]
Read it as: sk is the model’s score for character k. Dividing every score by T before the softmax leaves T = 1 as the model’s own belief; T < 1 exaggerates the gaps between scores, T > 1 shrinks them.
Say it“The probability of character k is e to the s-k over T, divided by the sum of the same over all characters.”
model’s surprise at its own text
words that are real Shakespeare words

3 · Look inside the gates

Every one of the LSTM’s 128 units has its own cell and gates. Nobody told any of them what to track, yet some found jobs a person can recognise (Karpathy, Johnson & Fei-Fei, 2016). We searched the held-out text for units whose cell value follows a simple property of the text; the presets below are the clearest finds. Below, a held-out passage is shaded by one unit’s value at every character. Pick a unit, choose what to show, and hover a character.

The same models in numpy

The reference below loads the same float16 weights the page uses and runs each model straight through the held-out text from a zero state, one character at a time, exactly as your browser does. The table above puts its numbers next to the browser’s.

import numpy as np
text  = open("input.txt").read()                       # Tiny Shakespeare, github.com/karpathy/char-rnn
chars = sorted(set(text)); ix = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(chars)}
data  = np.array([ix[c] for c in text]); cut = int(0.9 * len(data))
tr, val = data[:cut], data[cut:]
sig   = lambda a: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-a))

def step(cell, P, x, h, c):                            # one character in, new state out
    a = P["Wx"][x] + P["b"]; H = len(h)
    if cell == "rnn":
        return np.tanh(a + h @ P["Wh"]), c
    if cell == "lstm":
        a = a + h @ P["Wh"]
        i, f, o, g = sig(a[:H]), sig(a[H:2*H]), sig(a[2*H:3*H]), np.tanh(a[3*H:])
        c = f * c + i * g
        return o * np.tanh(c), c
    zr = sig(a[:2*H] + h @ P["Wh"][:, :2*H]); z, r = zr[:H], zr[H:]             # GRU
    n = np.tanh(a[2*H:] + (r * h) @ P["Wh"][:, 2*H:])
    return (1 - z) * h + z * n, c

def bits_per_char(cell, P, seq):
    h = c = np.zeros(P["Wh"].shape[0]); bits = 0.0
    for x, y in zip(seq[:-1], seq[1:]):
        h, c = step(cell, P, x, h, c); s = h @ P["Wy"] + P["by"]
        bits += (np.log(np.exp(s - s.max()).sum()) + s.max() - s[y]) / np.log(2)
    return bits / (len(seq) - 1)

uni = np.bincount(tr, minlength=65) + 1                # add-one counts
bi  = np.ones((65, 65)); np.add.at(bi, (tr[:-1], tr[1:]), 1)
for name, seq in [("excerpt", val[:5001]), ("all held-out", val)]:
    u = -np.log2(uni[seq[1:]] / uni.sum()).mean()
    b = -np.log2(bi[seq[:-1], seq[1:]] / bi[seq[:-1]].sum(1)).mean()
    print(f"{name:12s}  unigram {u:.4f}   bigram {b:.4f} bpc")

for cell in ["rnn", "gru", "lstm"]:
    P = {k: v.astype(np.float64) for k, v in np.load(f"rn_{cell}_f16.npz").items()}
    print(f"{cell:4s}  excerpt {bits_per_char(cell, P, val[:5001]):.4f} bpc   "
          f"all held-out {bits_per_char(cell, P, val):.4f} bpc")
excerpt       unigram 4.7709   bigram 3.5850 bpc
all held-out  unigram 4.8291   bigram 3.5806 bpc
rnn   excerpt 2.0877 bpc   all held-out 2.3331 bpc
gru   excerpt 1.9181 bpc   all held-out 2.2300 bpc
lstm  excerpt 1.9981 bpc   all held-out 2.3020 bpc

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • A recurrent network applies one small cell at every step, ht = tanh(W ht−1 + U xt + b), so the same weights read a sequence of any length and the state carries what came before.
  • Training unrolls the network into a deep net with shared weights and backpropagates through time; the gradient from step T to step k is a product of T − k Jacobians.
  • Products of many factors below 1 vanish and above 1 explode: plain RNNs rarely learn dependencies longer than a few dozen steps. Gradient clipping tames explosions, not vanishing.
  • The LSTM’s cell is updated by ct = f ⊙ ct−1 + i ⊙ g, so along the cell the gradient is multiplied only by forget gates; when f ≈ 1, memory and gradient both survive. The GRU gets the same effect with two gates and fewer weights.
  • Trained on raw characters, networks of 108,000 weights learn spelling, line breaks and speakers’ names. On held-out Shakespeare the gated cells beat a plain RNN of the same size (GRU 2.23, LSTM 2.30, RNN 2.33 bits per character, against 3.58 for letter pairs), and some LSTM units learn readable jobs, such as tracking the position in a line, that nobody assigned.

Check your understanding

An RNN reads a 1,000-step sequence. How many copies of W does it have, and how many layers does backpropagation go through?

One W, shared by every step. But unrolled, the computation is 1,000 layers deep, and the gradient for W is a sum of 1,000 contributions, one per step.

In a one-unit tanh RNN with w = 0.8, roughly how much of the gradient from 30 steps later reaches a state?

At most 0.830 ≈ 0.0012, and less still where tanh saturates, since each step also multiplies by 1 − h² ≤ 1. The nearby steps’ gradients are a thousand times louder.

Your RNN’s loss suddenly jumps to NaN during training. Which problem is this likely to be, and what is the cheap fix?

Exploding gradients: one huge gradient step threw the weights into a bad region. Clip the gradient’s norm (for example to 5) before each update; lowering the learning rate also helps.

Why does an LSTM’s gradient survive along the cell when an RNN’s does not?

Along the cell path, ∂ct/∂ct−1 = ft: there is no weight matrix and no squashing slope. The network can learn to hold f near 1 for as long as it needs to remember, so the product of forget gates stays near 1 instead of shrinking.

A GRU and an LSTM have 256 hidden units each and the same input. Which has more weights, and by how much?

The LSTM: it has four weight blocks (three gates and a candidate) to the GRU’s three (two gates and a candidate), so it has 4/3 as many weights in the recurrent layer.
